title: Supporting students through exam anxiety in the final stretch
description: A practical guide for Kenyan school principals and teachers on supporting students through the most intense anxiety period of the academic year, in the final weeks before major assessments.
body:
The final weeks before a major national assessment are when student anxiety reaches its peak in the Kenyan school calendar. This period requires deliberate, visible support from the school — not because students cannot manage pressure, but because well-supported students perform more consistently than those managing significant anxiety alone.

Recognise that anxiety at this stage is normal, not a weakness

A certain level of pre-assessment anxiety is a normal, even useful, physiological response that sharpens focus. The goal of support during this period is not to eliminate all anxiety, but to prevent it from escalating to a level that impairs a student's ability to function, sleep, and perform. Framing some anxiety as normal, while watching for signs of excessive distress, gives students permission to acknowledge their nerves without feeling they are failing to cope.

Practical, structured support

  • Brief, practical sessions on exam-day logistics and expectations reduce anxiety that stems from uncertainty about the unknown
  • Guidance counsellor availability specifically increased during this period, with visible, low-barrier access
  • Encouraging realistic, structured revision plans rather than panic-driven last-minute cramming, which tends to increase rather than reduce anxiety

A signal worth watching for: A student who was previously coping and suddenly shows signs of panic, withdrawal, or expressions of hopelessness in the final weeks needs immediate, gentle attention — not simply reassurance that "it will be fine," which can feel dismissive, but a genuine conversation about what support would actually help.

Managing the language used around students

Messaging that frames a single assessment as determining a student's entire future measurably increases anxiety without improving performance. Teachers and administrators who communicate confidence in students' preparation, alongside realistic and supportive expectations, contribute to calmer, more focused students than those who use pressure or fear as a primary motivational tool.

Practical coping strategies worth teaching directly

Simple techniques — structured breathing exercises, short physical breaks during long revision sessions, maintaining consistent sleep even under pressure to study longer — genuinely help students manage acute anxiety, but only if taught directly rather than assumed. A brief, practical session led by the guidance counsellor on these specific techniques gives students real tools, not just general encouragement.

Involving parents as partners during this period

A brief communication to parents ahead of the assessment period — encouraging them to support their child's wellbeing at home, maintain normal routines where possible, and avoid adding additional pressure through comparison with siblings or peers — extends the school's supportive approach into the home environment during the period when students spend significant time there.

Knowing when to refer for further support

Students showing signs of significant functional decline — unable to eat, sleep, attend classes, or engage at all — need support beyond what classroom-level intervention can provide. A clear, pre-established referral pathway to professional mental health support, as covered in our guide on student mental health, should be ready before this period begins, not improvised during it.
